title: What is the difference between the eager and cooperative-sticky rebalance protocols?
topicTitle: What is the difference between the eager and cooperative-sticky rebalance protoc

s1_definition.profdef: Eager and cooperative-sticky are the two rebalance protocols a Kafka consumer group uses to reassign partitions when membership changes. The eager protocol is stop-the-world: every consumer revokes all its partitions, then the group recomputes and reassigns everything from scratch, so all consumers pause during the rebalance. The cooperative-sticky protocol is incremental: consumers keep the partitions they already own, and only the specific partitions that must move are revoked and reassigned, usually over two short rebalances, so most consumers keep processing throughout.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India reassigning counters among tellers when a new teller joins. Eager rebalancing is like telling every teller to leave their counter and stand in the hallway, then handing out counter assignments again from scratch — the whole bank stops serving customers during the reshuffle. Cooperative-sticky rebalancing is like saying "most of you keep your current counters; only two counters need to move to the new teller," so almost everyone keeps serving customers and only the few affected counters pause briefly.
s1_definition.oneliner: Eager revokes all partitions and pauses the whole group; cooperative-sticky keeps existing assignments and only moves the partitions that truly need to move.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Eager and cooperative-sticky are the two rebalance protocols a Kafka consumer group uses to reassign partitions when membership changes. The eager protocol is stop-the-world: every consumer revokes all its partitions, then the group recomputes and reassigns everything from scratch, so all consumers pause during the rebalance. The cooperative-sticky protocol is incremental: consumers keep the partitions they already own, and only the specific partitions that must move are revoked and reassigned, usually over two short rebalances, so most consumers keep processing throughout.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India reassigning counters among tellers when a new teller joins. Eager rebalancing is like telling every teller to leave their counter and stand in the hallway, then handing out counter assignments again from scratch — the whole bank stops serving customers during the reshuffle. Cooperative-sticky rebalancing is like saying "most of you keep your current counters; only two counters need to move to the new teller," so almost everyone keeps serving customers and only the few affected counters pause briefly.

**One line to remember:** Eager revokes all partitions and pauses the whole group; cooperative-sticky keeps existing assignments and only moves the partitions that truly need to move.

sections.s2_technical:
A rebalance happens whenever group membership or topic metadata changes: a consumer joins, a consumer leaves or crashes, or partitions are added. The protocol decides how disruptive that reassignment is.

The eager protocol, implemented by assignors like `RangeAssignor` and `RoundRobinAssignor`, works in one phase. Every consumer first revokes all of its currently owned partitions, which means it stops consuming and commits offsets. Then the group leader computes a brand-new assignment and every consumer picks up its newly assigned partitions. The problem is that even a consumer whose partitions do not change still gives them up and reacquires them, so the entire group experiences a processing pause for the duration of the rebalance. In a large group this stop-the-world pause can be significant and shows up as a latency spike.

The cooperative-sticky protocol, implemented by the `CooperativeStickyAssignor`, works incrementally and tries to keep assignments stable. On the first rebalance it computes the desired assignment and only revokes the partitions that need to move to a different consumer. The consumers that keep their partitions never stop. A second short rebalance then assigns the freed partitions to their new owners. Because most partitions stay put, only the migrating partitions pause, and the sticky behaviour means that after a transient blip the group tends to return to a similar assignment, avoiding needless churn.

You select the protocol with the `partition.assignment.strategy` consumer property, for example `partition.assignment.strategy=org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.CooperativeStickyAssignor`. In Spring Kafka you set it under consumer properties. There is a migration caution: you cannot mix an eager assignor and a cooperative assignor in the same group abruptly, because they disagree on whether to revoke everything. The supported path is a rolling upgrade where you first deploy consumers configured with both the old and the cooperative assignor, then a second deploy with only cooperative.

The senior nuances are these. Cooperative-sticky dramatically reduces the impact of routine events like a single consumer restart or a deployment rollout, which is exactly what you want in a bank running continuous deployments. It uses the `ConsumerRebalanceListener` callbacks `onPartitionsRevoked` and `onPartitionsAssigned`, plus `onPartitionsLost` for the incremental case, and you should commit offsets in `onPartitionsRevoked` so no work is double-processed. Static group membership, set with `group.instance.id`, complements cooperative rebalancing by letting a briefly restarting consumer rejoin without triggering any rebalance at all within the session timeout.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs a settlement consumer group with ten consumers reading a transfers topic of twelve partitions. Every time they deploy a new version, which is several times a day, each consumer restarts in turn. Under the eager protocol, each restart caused the entire group to stop processing for a few seconds, producing visible latency spikes on settlement. This is exactly the stop-the-world cost of eager rebalancing.

Problem 2 — The team switched to the cooperative-sticky assignor. Now when one consumer restarts during a deploy, only that consumer's partitions move; the other nine keep processing without interruption. This is exactly the incremental benefit of cooperative-sticky rebalancing.

We simulate both protocols in plain Java. A `RebalanceSimulator` holds an assignment of partitions to consumers and supports a consumer leaving. Under eager mode it revokes everything and reassigns from scratch; under cooperative mode it keeps existing owners and only moves the departed consumer's partitions. The demo prints how many partitions were paused in each case. The code will show: a `Consumer` holder, the `RebalanceSimulator` with both modes, and a demo removing one consumer under each protocol.

```yaml
# application.yml — real Spring Kafka cooperative-sticky config
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: localhost:9092
    consumer:
      group-id: settlement
      properties:
        partition.assignment.strategy: org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.CooperativeStickyAssignor
        group.instance.id: ${HOSTNAME}      # static membership reduces rebalances
        session.timeout.ms: 45000
        max.poll.interval.ms: 300000
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a settlement group of four consumers over twelve partitions, then consumer settle-2 leaves.

Step 1: The initial assignment spreads twelve partitions across four consumers, three each. Consumer settle-2 owns three partitions.

Step 2: Under the eager protocol, settle-2 leaving triggers a stop-the-world rebalance. Every consumer revokes all of its partitions, so all twelve partitions pause, even the nine owned by consumers that are not leaving.

Step 3: The group leader recomputes a fresh assignment across the remaining three consumers, four partitions each, and everyone resumes. The pause affected the entire topic.

Step 4: Under the cooperative-sticky protocol, settle-2 leaving only orphans its three partitions. The other three consumers keep their existing partitions and never stop.

Step 5: The three orphaned partitions are handed to the remaining consumers in a short second rebalance, so only three partitions paused and nine kept processing throughout.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The eager and cooperative-sticky protocols are two ways a consumer group redistributes partitions when its membership changes, and the difference is how disruptive that redistribution is. The eager protocol is stop-the-world. When anything changes, every consumer revokes all of its partitions, the group recomputes a fresh assignment, and then everyone picks up their new partitions. The problem is that even consumers whose partitions do not change still give them up and take them back, so the entire group pauses for the duration of the rebalance, which shows up as a latency spike.

The cooperative-sticky protocol is incremental. Consumers keep the partitions they already own, and only the specific partitions that genuinely need to move to a different consumer are revoked, usually over two short rebalances. The consumers that keep their partitions never stop, so only the migrating partitions pause. The sticky part means the group tends to return to a similar assignment after a transient blip instead of churning. You select it with the partition assignment strategy property set to the cooperative-sticky assignor.

The practical reason this matters in a bank is continuous deployment. If I deploy several times a day and each consumer restarts in turn, the eager protocol makes the whole settlement group stall briefly on every single restart, while cooperative-sticky confines the pause to just that one consumer's partitions. I pair it with static group membership using a group instance id so that a consumer that restarts quickly rejoins within the session timeout without triggering any rebalance at all. The migration caution I always mention is that you cannot flip the whole group from eager to cooperative at once, because the assignors disagree on revocation; you do a rolling upgrade that first lists both assignors, then a second deploy with cooperative only.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, our settlement consumers originally used an eager assignor and every rolling deploy produced visible settlement latency spikes because the whole group stopped during each consumer restart. We moved to the cooperative-sticky assignor with static membership, and now a deploy only pauses the handful of partitions owned by the consumer being restarted while the rest keep settling trades. The senior framing I give is that in a system with frequent deploys and strict latency expectations, the rebalance protocol is not a minor tuning knob; choosing cooperative-sticky turns a routine restart from a group-wide outage into a localized, barely noticeable event.
